name: Ian Bremmer
role: American political scientist, Eurasia Group founder and GZERO Media president
summary: Bremmer supports international cooperation, competitive enterprise and social protection for people excluded from economic gains. His policy recommendations emphasize climate coordination, AI governance and limits on executive power; he distinguishes his geopolitical forecasts from personal preferences.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Insists rapid AI deployment requires safeguards and governance against catastrophic misuse.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Says fiscal stimulus is right in recessions and that deficit spending that builds long-term assets (education, health, infrastructure, decarbonization) is fine, while urging tightening in booms.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Accepts creative destruction as an engine of growth while demanding protection for those harmed.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: He expressly condemns the Russian military for unjustly making Ukrainian civilians targets and calls the harm to those civilians a reason to pay attention to the invasion.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Bremmer reports that many ethnic Russians in Crimea regarded the peninsula as part of greater Russia. He says the local attachment to Russia and Moscow’s historical ties give Russia no basis to disregard Ukrainian sovereignty under international law.

collective-defense.rationale: Stresses Article 5, that allies answered it after 9/11, and says an Article 5-style tripwire is needed for deterrence; doubt over US commitment is a gift to Moscow.

corporate-influence.rationale: Criticizes lobbying and privileged political access that let the wealthy buy opportunities.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Defends courts’ ability to restrain a popularly elected executive.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Insists people disadvantaged by globalization need support and regrets prospective subsidy cuts.

decide-locally.rationale: Praises state-level decision-making as a source of American resilience.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Mixed: he earlier proposed major public climate investment, but more recently emphasizes energy innovation and says global climate governance is unnecessary.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Defends NATO’s value and criticizes policies undermining its coherence.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Makes preventing catastrophic AI-driven conflict a central reason for international governance.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Includes nuclear expansion among necessary post-carbon energy solutions.

experts-over-public.rationale: Wants expert-directed AI governance insulated from politicians’ limited expertise and electoral time horizons.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: He argues that reducing commercial interdependence between China and the United States would lower the cost of going to war and raise the risk of direct military confrontation.

gradual-change.rationale: Calls necessary political disruption an opportunity rather than something to fear.

human-caused-global-warming.rationale: In his discussion of The Power of Crisis he attributes present warming to human activity and explicitly rules out natural cycles as the explanation.

language-defines-nation.rationale: His account of post-Soviet Ukraine identifies a distinct Ukrainian national identity among people whose linguistic and ethnic backgrounds overlap extensively with Russia’s, including ethnic Ukrainians in predominantly Russian-speaking Kharkiv.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He describes regulated free markets as relatively more efficient than state capitalism and argues that displacement of global markets by state-directed markets reduces efficiency and growth.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: He urges European countries to commit troops to guarantee Ukraine’s security after a ceasefire, even without a US backstop.

national-mission.rationale: On returning to his Superpower argument in 2017, he recommends that the United States rebuild at home and lead by example instead of trying to run the international system or engineer political outcomes abroad.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Advocates government responsibilities in social protection, research and climate policy.

no-central-bank.rationale: In Dealing with Uncertainty, chapter 2 of The Fat Tail, Bremmer and Keat credit the Federal Reserve with averting a financial crisis after the September 11 attacks. In his own column Bremmer treats an independent central bank as a foundation of confidence in the dollar.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Calls American politics kleptocratic and dominated by money.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: After the attempted assassination of Donald Trump, he said a democracy cannot tolerate political violence in any form and called on people across the political spectrum to condemn it.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Proposes shared digital rules, a permanent secretariat and international judicial enforcement.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: He argues that Western governments should have actively helped post-Soviet Russia build a democratic market economy and integrated it into international institutions.

proportional-representation.rationale: Answering a question about multi-party proportional representation, says a multi-party system would be a constructive development, while doubting it can be achieved.

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: He condemns recognizing Russia’s illegally annexed Ukrainian territory and defends territorial integrity against the view that military power can settle borders.

religious-nation.rationale: Asked about the merits of Christian nationalism, he rejects it and says governing on the basis of strong religious beliefs is exclusionary.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Says in his view President Trump should be removed from office (impeached) for weaponized disinformation about the election, favoring the constitutional route.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Insists policies can succeed despite his rejection of the politician responsible; separates assessment from preference.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Calls on wealthy Japan to coordinate humanitarian assistance for people and governments in need.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Lists gay marriage among the liberties he says he supports, in his own column and on camera (2021).

separate-church-state.rationale: He explicitly endorses separation of church and state when asked about parties that campaign on defending Christian traditions.

separated-powers.rationale: Wants an independent judiciary to constrain executive abuses.

social-market-economy.rationale: Wants American growth combined with stronger European-style social protection.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Treats executive refusal to obey judicial rulings as a constitutional danger.

space-expansion.rationale: Prioritizes caring for people on Earth over business leaders’ ambitions for Mars.

state-harmful.rationale: Treats effective public institutions and social protection as necessary.

state-laws-apply-online.rationale: He calls for comprehensive federal privacy legislation to limit the collection and misuse of Americans’ personal data by online platforms and other companies.

strong-leader.rationale: Opposes executive attacks on constitutional restraints despite acknowledging some effective policies.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Condemns weaponizing justice, tax and investigative agencies against political enemies.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Rejects sweeping protective tariffs as economically damaging.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Expresses optimism that new technology creates solutions faster than problems, while recognizing risks.

trade-surplus.rationale: Rejects treating bilateral deficits as proof that trade partners exploit America.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Condemns combining immense private wealth, presidential patronage and public administrative power.

notes:
Forecasts, interview questions, guests’ views and descriptions of voter attitudes are not treated as personal preferences. The 2019 climate-investment recommendation is qualified by the August 2026 emphasis on innovation rather than global climate governance. Political revolution refers to institutional transformation such as Roosevelt’s, not an endorsement of violence. Specific speech, religious and immigration policies remain unknown without direct evidence. All remaining null statements reviewed; no living-person inferences.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 9 answers taken from it, 12 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass, from his own words only: about 1,030 GZERO Media pages (his 'by Ian Bremmer' columns and Q&As, Quick Takes, Ask Ian, Ian Explains), downloaded and searched by theme, and 820 of his CNN/NPR interview turns 2001-2020 (MediaSum). Forecasts, analysis of what leaders will do and descriptions of what voters want were not counted as positions. Themes searched: economy (health, tax, minimum wage, deficits, trade, UBI), government (elections, courts, executive power, money in politics, term limits), world (NATO, UN, EU, intervention, Israel, China, sanctions, arms control), liberty (speech, guns, drugs, privacy, surveillance), society (abortion, marriage, immigration), ecology and technology. Marijuana support does not settle drugs generally; support for skilled immigration does not settle overall levels; his support for free speech and verified human accounts does not settle hate-speech law or anonymity; platform liability and privacy-law comments do not settle corporate regulation in general; AI-governance remarks do not settle existential-risk priority. Abortion, healthcare, minimum wage, basic income, death penalty, Israel and Taiwan: only analysis, no stated preference. The earlier pass checked Internet Archive for five books. The later pass records those works and additional access attempts in notFound. No answer rests on what a government did rather than on his own words.

November 2026 pass searched the local GZERO columns and transcripts, MediaSum interview turns, the local text of The Fat Tail, book previews and Carnegie Council interviews. The review covered fiscal and monetary policy, labor, elections, constitutional power, war and alliances, international law, political violence, migration, ethnic and national identity, church and state, climate and technology. Read the authors’ evaluation of central-bank crisis response in The Fat Tail and used it with Bremmer’s own account of the dollar.
